An FPGA is a grid you configure

You will learn

What an FPGA is made of, and why a design uses only part of the chip.

A CPU runs instructions one after another. An FPGA has no program at all: it is a grid of small blocks -- lookup tables (LUTs), flip-flops, carry chains, block RAM and DSP multipliers -- joined by wires you can switch. Configuring the grid builds a circuit. Our bench chip is an AMD Artix-7 XC7A200T on an ALINX AX7203 board, in the 484-ball FBG484 package. The skyline draws one routed design on that die: every tile it configures stands up as a column, and most of the chip stays dark.

Try it

Rotate the die and tap the tallest column: which kind of tile sets the most features? The spec frame is the board file of a Wukong, which carries the same die: find LUT_TOTAL. It holds AMD's logic cell count, 1.6 per LUT6, not a LUT count. Then find the invariant on DSP48E1_TOTAL: what does its name say our cores use?
